speechtext:
I do not believe it, but I am going to call these opponents to time. I am not only going to name Lord Atholstan but I also name the president of the Bank of Montreal and the president of the Royal Bank, both of whom are directors of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. I am also going to (Challenge the whole organization of the Canadian Pacific Railway to say whether or not they are working to-day to destroy the Canadian National Railway system and put it out of business, in order to acquire it to their own company. I challenge all these people to say whether that is the object they have in mind. I have seen a good deal of their hand at work in the last election, as well as some other organizations in which they are interested. One such organization is that which they have in Montreal at Garden City-I think it is called the Railway Users Association. They are now distributing propaganda throughout 24011-31
this country; they say they are railway users, but I say they are agents of-and I will use a term which has been used before-the St. James street group of Montreal. If it is true that Montreal as a city and Quebec as a province are against the National railways, the sooner the headquarters of the Canadian National are taken out of that city and brought to Ottawa the better for the people of Canada.
Having said that, I am going to take up another phase of the situation and deal with the question of public ownership. We know what public ownership is in Ontario. We have a hydro-electric system which is the admiration of all the world, which is publicly owned and in which there is no profit. We have public ownership there; we have public ownership in the street railway system and the motor bus service of Toronto, and I am told that they are going to supplement that service by a system of taxis at cheap rates. It is said that the Montreal group not only hates public ownership but hates it especially >in the way it has manifested itself in Ontario. But we have more than that; Ontario has a splendid railway called the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario Railway, which opened up the silver fields and the new gold fields of Ontario and which has given an impetus to the opening of the Rouyn field in Quebec. Ontario has set an example to all the other provinces in the way of building its own roads to open up the province. We have many other instances of public ownership; in the eyes of some it is apparently a crime to advocate such a thing, but sentiment favourable to that policy is growing all over the country. I want to tell this House now-and I hope hon. gentlemen will ponder it well-that the great proposition before the-world to-day is to take the profiteering out of the great public services and to distribute those services at cost to the people who participate in them. That is the underlying principle. One of the first persons who, in a public way, has taken it up is Mr.'Baruch of New York, whom I believe to be a German by birth. He has given a large sum of money towards the development of the idea of taking profiteering out of war. Profiteering was one of the causes of that disastrous war through which we recently passed. Hundreds and thousands of fortunes were made out of that war, not only on this continent but also on the continent of Europe, and that is the menace of the world to-day. People are awakening to that fact, not only here but to a greater degree in the United States, and they are beginning to advocate the removal of profiteering from

4S2	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Maclean (York)
the great public services. What I mean by profiteering is dividends for shareholders as against bank interest on the money involved.
I want to give a recent example of public ownership that will probably astound this House, and I am going to give it on my responsibility as a citizen, a very ordinary citizen of this country. After a good deal of investigation I find that undoubtedly the greatest instance of public ownership to-day is the National Reserve bank system of the United States. And this is where I issue my challenge to the Wall Street Journal: The National Reserve bank system of the United States has in its possession for the people of that country billions of gold in bars or in coinage, other millions in coinage subsidiary of gold, and it has an unlimited number of its own notes. The best money in the world is the national note of the people of the United States issued from the treasury at Washington. And this great banking organization is doing-and this is where it comes in as a public ownership proposition-what the United States to-day, through its treasury organization and the National bank reserve, is doing, namely, all the rediscounting for all the banks of the United States at actual cost. Does my right hon. friend laugh at that?

maintopic: GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
No, I have a humorist
behind me.

maintopic: GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
It is the greatest example in the world to-day of public ownership; and I challenge the Wall Street Journal to say it is not true that the treasury of the United States and the National Reserve bank are now doing the rediscounting for all the banks of the republic and doing it at cost. They have taken the profiteering out of the rediscount proposition in the United States, and it is one of the surprising things of the world. What they have done is to the credit of the government of the United States and also the people of that country. They have encouraged all the little local banks; every one of them, if it amounts to anything, has to become a member-bank of the reserve bank system. Not one of those member-banks dares default for a moment, and none does default; the money is always there. And so the local banks of the United States are getting the rediscounting of all their business paper at cost, a service rendered by the National Reserve bank system. Now that is the first and largest illustration that I can give of public ownership applied to the solution of a great problem. Behind that National Reserve bank system there are all the stores of gold and silver that the United States possesses. The

republic has also billions of notes and obligations from all over the world that they have taken in connection with the .war, and all that money is consecrated to the National Reserve bank system. They have all this paper, too, that they hold under discount. There is a great outstanding example to our friends in Montreal who say they do not believe in public ownership of railways in Canada,
I had to go to the United States for that illustration, and now I am going to cite something further. Alongside the National Reserve bank system in the United States there is the Interstate Commerce Commission. However, before I deal with that I want to go back a little. I do not know that the United States owns a single bank share, yet it has absolute mastery of the whole banking System of that country. I do not believe the United States owns a single mile of railway, although perhaps it does own some little lines here and there. But the United States, to-day through its Interstate Commerce Commission, which is an absolute public ownership service, is administering the railroads of the republic and compelling them to organize and consolidate themselves into larger systems. The movement was started a while ago to force them to organize into twelve groups. That number is being reduced, and another great merger went through the other day. Before long the railways there will fee so closely merged that the United 'States will be in complete control, and later practically in complete ownership of the railway system of that great country. Well now, I have given those examples of public ownership. It may be said "Oh, that is not public ownership." Well, what is it?

maintopic: GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Public control.

maintopic: GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
It is more than
public control; it is public service, and that is another thing than public control. Over there they have this great public service and: by it they are able to regulate and fix the-rate of interest and discount. That is what the United States National Reserve bank has; been doing for the last few months. Every time the bank statement comes out it can be seen that the rate of interest is going down, and that is being done by the great institution which I have mentioned. We have got control and some regulation of the banks in this; country, but I want to tell the people of' Montreal-and I am coming to banking now for a moment-living as we do alongside of the United States, that unless we give the same public service that they are giving in regard to banking-and we do give the same service in regard to railways-it will not bn

The Address-Mr. Maclean (York)
long before Canadians will be asking why we have not the same banking system that the United States have.
The heads of two great banks of Canada, Sir Vincent Meredith and Sir Herbert Holt, have made a great success of their banking. But if they are going to obstruct the public ownership of railways in this country the people of Canada will demand that there ibe further banking amendments here to create a national reserve bank system such as they have in the United States,, especially for the encouragement of local banks, instead of what they call the bank branch system. I pass from these gentlemen to a very clever bank manager, Mr. Neill of the Royal Bank of Canada. Mr. Neill has undertaken to lecture me and you, and the rest of the people of Canada, and to argue that the branch bank system is better than the system of local banks and that the Canadian plan is ahead of the United States plan. I challenge that here and now, and I say that Canada has got to have a banking system similar to what they have in the United States. I am going to make an appeal to the patriotism of our people. Not long ago the Prime Minister of Great Britain, Mr. Baldwin, made an expedition to the United States to settle the war debt of Great Britain to that country. He effected a settlement, and it was all done more or less through the National Reserve bank system of the United States. If Canada had a similar system we could have done a great deal for the credit of the Mother Country, and done it probably in association with the banking system of the United States.
We were talking about via medias the other day. That is one thing that is available. Already the rumour has gone abroad that the national reserve bank system of the United States wants to open a branch in Canada, and if we do not open our own system, they will come here from the States, and you will find brokers opening up in Canada before long; they will undertake to collect great blocks of paper for discount in Canada, take it over to the United States and rediscount it there. I am perhaps going out of my way, and it is rather an adventure for me. I am telling these men who are directors of the Canadian Pacific Railway and who are heads of the great banking systems which are organized in Montreal, that if they persist- even if they disclaim being participants in the attack on the Canadian National Railways- that we are going to follow the United1 States in adopting what we think is an improved system of banking in this country for rediscounting in the local banks. Of course I want to see the big banks remain, but I want to 34011-31J
see local banks provided in the small communities for the development of the industries of their local people. Something in that direction will be only a step in the direction of the creation of farm credits, and that is the most dangerous thing we have to deal with. But there is some connection between them.
I have made an analysis of and dealt with the various agencies that we have for transportation in this country, I have dealt w'th the opposition to the National Railways, and I say that these men in Montreal-and for short I call them the St. James street group-they or somebody in Montreal are at the bottom of that Railway Users' Association. I challenge them to a show-down, to say where they stand in connection with the Canadian National Railways and whether they really believe the people of Quebec and the Premier of Quebec are determined to block the National Railways, to turn them over to the Canadian Pacific Railways and to smash them. No charge can be made against hon. members on this side. The consolidation of our railways was carried out by Sir Robert Borden and Sir Thomas White and by the present leader of the opposition here. We have the National Railways on our hands, and have to make good, and thank God the surprising thing to the world to-day is the manner in which the Canadian National Railways are making good. Where is the man who will stand up in this House and say he endorses the destructive campaign, the inimical campaign, directed by the Montreal press and by Atholstan and by the Whites to destroy the National Railways? Is there any hon. member of this House who will justify it?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Oh, no.

maintopic: GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
No, nor will anyone in the House say that he is against the National Railways. No one on this side of the House will say it, because we are all1 proud of the National Railways and of the service Sir Henry Thornton has given us. I desire to give the government credit for what they have done. They have advanced large sums to the Canadian National Railways, and I do not think they are going to lose anything by it. The service is increasing, the Canadian people are taking pride in their own railway and are patronizing it the more because it is impressed on them that the Canadian Pacific is behind this attack that is made upon it.
I come now to the Canadian Pacific Railway. I am not the oldest man in the House, but I came to this House as a young newspaperman almost fifty years ago, and even at
484	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Maclean (York)
that time I knew, although not very intimately, a man who became one of the greatest men in Canada; my father knew him very well. 1 refer to George Stephen., as he was then called. I saw that Canadian Pacific railway system grow up and George Stephen, afterwards Lord Mount-Stephen, a Scotchman by birth but a splendid Canadian, who got in touch with Sir John A. Macdonald. Do hon. members know how George Stephen got in *touch with Sir John A.? He was engaged in textile industries in this country and he got into various lines of woollens at first, then cotton, and in connection with Sir John A.'s National Policy which was the beginning of the industrial organization of Canada-

maintopic: GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: The prosperity of Canada.

maintopic: GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Yes. He got
into touch with Sir John A. Macdonald; and George Stephen, a man doing business in connection with textiles, rose to the opportunity and organized the original Canadian Pacific syndicate. He and his associates made the contract for the Canadian Pacific Railway. That Canadian Pacific Railway was built and it is one Of the most successful Railways in the world to-day. I give these men credit for what they did. Then associated with Lord Mount Stephen was Donald Smith, and I even remember seeing Donald Smith here in Ottawa, a representative of the Hudson Bay Company; he knew all about our west. And one of the Anguses was here then. Those men were interested in Canada, had faith in Canada, they knew the west and knew what railways had done for the development of the western states. These men got together and built the Canadian Pacific Railway, and it has been a magnificent success. It has given great service. It opened up the country. I believe the rates were high, and that they were pretty hard on the patrons of that road in the past, but the rates came under the jurisdiction of the railway commission and the road gives just as good service, so far as the charges go, as the Canadian National Railways. I appreciate the fact that these gentlemen I have named and the newspapers I have referred to have every confidence in the Canadian Pacific Railway. So have I. But in connection with the Canadian Pacific and the consolidation of the other railway lines in Canada, a new problem has come to this country. We went on a mad venture of over-railroading in Canada in the past. We built three transcontinental lines, if not more, when one or two would have been enough. We went on

building railways in the west, and then we started, when we brought the Canadian Pacific Railway down here, to duplicate the existing roads of all the country. And so this country to-day is cursed-and I use this term advisedly-with a duplication of railway systems which is absolutely unnecessary and which is costing the country to-day over two hundred million dollars a year. The loss to-day on account of this absolutely unnecessary duplication of railways in Canada is fully that amount. I am not merely speaking by guesswork; I have some authority for what I am saying.

maintopic: GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Annually?

maintopic: GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Yes; the loss on account of the unnecessary duplication- is over two hundred million dollars annually. The House and the country must approach this railway problem in a broad way. If the Canadian Pacific Railway thinks it is the bigger dog and can eat up the other one, that is the end of the matter. But I believe the Canadian Pacific Railway to-day (is ready to treat with the Canadian National Railways for the removal of these unnecessary duplications in order to put the two great systems together into one, namely the Canadian National Railways. When that is done, you get a great steamship service that is paying its way. You are on the ocean with all kinds of steamers. This is -where I began this debate last year when the government across the way proposed to this House that we should give enormous subsidies to the Petersen syndicate. I said!: No; instead of taking new money out of the treasury in order to solve the ocean transportation problem, make an arrangement with the Canadian Pacific for consolidation with the Canadian National and, in that way, get a great steamship service, not only on the Atlantic and the Pacific, -but on our Great Lakes and rivers. You will then begin really to solve the transportation problem in a big way without increasing your liabilities. That idea was not taken up then, and although I am rather afraid to make the suggestion, I am going to make -it: that if this House is big enough for its opportunities-and the opportunity is here now to clean up this transportation problem, to cut out these unnecessary duplications and to get a better service on the ocean-the only way in which to bring this about is to approach the Canadian Pacific Railway -in a fair manner and to make a reasonable arrangement by which not only the duplication I have mentioned, but the duplication involved in

The Address-Mr. Maclean (York)
having two systems, shall end. If the two roads are put together, you can do-and this is something new, I hope-what engineers call re-routing. If these two railway systems were turned over to a corps of good engineers, they would immediately re-route the transcontinental and branch line services, taking the best out of either system, putting them together, choosing the best grades, the best bridges and the best locations in the different towns and cities. If that were done, millions of dollars a year would be saved, the service would be improved and a great deal of railway material would be scrapped. What would come of that? We are over-railroaded in the east and in large portions of the west; but if we can scrap 5,000 miles of unnecessary railway trackage in the west, we have 5,000 miles of rails, 5,000 miles of ballast, 5,000 miles of ties and all the stations and freight houses to put into the Canadian National railways in building new lines in the west where they are wanted for the new settlers we propose to bring out to that part of the country.

maintopic: GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman state in what part of the west these lines could be torn up?

maintopic: GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
No. I want the western men to decide that; but I will give them the material. I am not going to settle any of these problems. I am only trying to approach them as a member of this House and to assume my responsibility of dealing with these problems as they exist. We have the problem involved in our being over-railroaded in this country. We have the problem of finding railways in the west for the new settlers we hope to bring to this country- because if we are going to build up Canada, we want more settlers and more wheat fields. The greatest asset we have now is our wheat fields in the west, and they will be a still greater asset when Winnipeg, Edmonton and other progressive cities in western Canada will have industrial populations around them making a market for the local farmers in addition to the markets of the world.
All these things have to be looked at in a broad way, and I am going to make this suggestion:	We have heard a good deal about
co-operation between two parties in this House as a coming solution of our difficulties, and I admit we have difficulties. But I say that the time has come when all the representatives of the people of Canada in this House must sit down together and see how our railway problem can be solved without any unjust or unfair treatment of the Canadian
Pacific. I have the greatest admiration for what the Canadian Pacific has done. They have been largely the victims of the overbuilding of railways that this parliament has encouraged in Canada. We must treat them fairly; we must solve our railway problem, and the only way of solving it is by the cooperation of the different parties in thi3 House. We have had too much partyism in this chamber of late and, as I say, we have heard a good deal of talk about co-operation. I am ready to co-operate with anybody or any party in this House who will deal with this problem, bring about a settlement, put our National railway on its feet, and cut out this unnecessary duplication including duplicate express and telegraph services. I happened to tell a fridnd of mine, who is very much interested in the railway problem, that I was going to bring this matter up and he said: "Maclean, you will get an awful spanking if you do." I am ready to take the spanking, and I hope other hon. gentlemen are ready to sit down together and, first of all, to settle this problem of transportation.
We have had one great experience to widen our view of things. We did not go through the war without being able to take an after-the-war view of problems. The after-the-war view of problems is absolutely necessary as a solution of our political troubles. I could speak on that topic all night, but I am not going to do so. I very much appreciate the attention which 'hon. members have given me and I have just one thing to say about this House: I have seen every parliament since the sixth in this House and this is the fifteenth I have known nine parliaments in this House and the largest representation of young men has arrived in this parliament to-day. They are here now and they are the spes gentis of Canada. They are the hope of the nation. I want to see them come forward and I congratulate these young men who are now in this House. They are making good speeches; indeed, the model maiden speech was made in this House last night by the hon. member for South Toronto (Mr. Geary). It was not a long speech, but it was an able one. Perhaps it was studied a little, but it was none the worse for that. I compliment these newcomers and I want to tell them, especially the 'hon. member for South Toronto, the hon. member for Toronto West Centre (Mr. Hocken), the hon. member for East Toronto (Mr. Ryck-man) and the hon. member for Toronto Northwest (Mr. Church) with his aspirations, that their aspirations should not be dampened because they see a solid phalanx of twelve exministers sitting on the front benches. It is
486	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Maclean (York)
rather an intimation that these are the reserved seats for the ministers of the next Conservative cabinet, but I want to tell the young men of the House that that is not so. How they got there, I do not know; but they are there and they think they are entrenched in reserved seats. May I say to these promising young men that there is hope for them and the way to accomplish their ambition is to make short speeches, speeches like that which the hon. member for South Toronto made last night. They must also practise the parliamentary trick. It is a very hard thing to become proficient in parliament and I am not boasting of being in any way proficient myself. These young men are better Canadians than any of us who are older and they fully appreciate what it is to be a Canadian. But I too appreciate the privileges and the responsibilities of Canadian citizenship and when I speak of co-operation I want it understood that I speak not so much as a citizen of Ontario as I do as a son of upper Canada who is willing to co-operate with the sons of lower Canada. It was the sons of lower Canada who in the old days joined with us of upper Canada in the salvation of this country. There is the formula, if you want it, for the settlement of the difficulties of former days. Probably we shall not have an opportunity in this House to settle the tariff issue, but there is no reason Why we should not settle our railway problem without a dissolution. Some people talk about the dissolution; who is going to bring it about? The fellows who talk about it cannot do it; they think they can but they cannot. We may 'have to hold up the settlement of the tariff question for some time but there are other things that we can deal with. And speaking of the tariff, I am going to vote for the amendment. I come from a constituency made up largely of market gardeners, fruit growers, florists, poultrymen and butchers who all derive their main livelihood from the business they do in the city of Toronto, and the amendment covers in a measure their views in regard to the tariff. I know of course that it contradicts the views held by western people who wrant the benefit of the early products of the United States and elsewhere; they want the early vegetables. I cannot deny that, and that is one of the problems that we shall have to solve. I am quite aware, as I speak even now, that I may be severely criticized in my own town for saying that the tariff issue may have to hang fire for a while, but I do not see anything else for it.
Now if I have said anything to hurt the feelings of those who are associated with the
{Mr. W. F. Maclean.]
banking system in Montreal or of those connected with the Canadian Pacific Railway, I will apologize at once. It occurs to me however-indeed, I have read the statement- that the Canadian 'National railway system is regarded by some people in Canada as a stone about the neck of this country. I deny that suggestion and I hurl it back at those who make it; and the last man at whom I hurl it is the representative of the. 'Mond Nickel Company, and the man who controls those mines in my province at Sudbury. That gentleman, in a lecture to the Canadian club, which was reported in that great enemy of public ownership the Toronto Financial Post, after surveying the situation in Canada deplored the evil of our railway debt and the dole system that exists in Canada. I want to tell Mr. Corless, and I want to tell Sir Alfred Mond who owns the nickel mines in Sudbury, as I do also notify the International Nickel Company, that if they want to help Canada the best thing for them to do is to develop these nickel mines by refining the nickel and making of it a finished product in this country instead of shipping out the raw material for the development of either England or the United States. I will not go into that question to-day, but it must be obvious to all hon. gentlemen that the only means by which this country is to be developed is to compel those who own these natural resources,-and Canada has a monopoly of them -whether it be nickel, asbestos, aluminum or even pulpwood, to put all these materials through the complete process of manufacture from the raw state to the finished product so as to give work to our Canadian people and freight to our Canadian railways.

maintopic: GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The hon. member who has just sat down (Mr. Maclean, York) by his reference to some of the problems that face the Canadian people to-day must have reminded us that in this country of diversified interests the people of one part necessarily look at these things from a different standpoint from that of the people in other portions of the country. I think however that it must be gratifying to the whole of Canada that since the last parliament we have been enjoying a greater measure of prosperity than has been our lot at any time since the war. This has been due mostly to an abundant production on the farms. But not only amongst agriculturists themselves is there greater hope and less despair; this hope and courage are apparent in our industrial centres as well. The basic industry of agriculture has proved the one great producer of wealth in this Dominion. In the years 1922

The Address-Mr. Evans
and 1923, and perhaps later, when the so-called "whispers of death" were heard over the land, when emigration was taking place to an extent unsurpassed in the history of Canada, it is very significant that agriculture was the one thing that caused a return to prosperity. The general progress and prosperity of any country is fairly well measured in modern times by the extent of that country's railway traffic, and a review of the tonnage carried in Canada brings to light the startling fact that while this basic industry of agriculture has for many years been bled and sacrificed to the one idea of building up the industrial centres, it is at present the only industry which we may expect to contribute very materially to a returning prosperity in Canada. Agriculture in this country has long been hampered through the fallacy that the progress of Canada depended on the development of the centres of industry, and unjust burdens of taxation have consequently been placed upon the primary producer; but we find now that agriculture has been the only industry that has advanced since 1913, the year before the Great War. We find that in 1924 the railways carried 27,979,000 tons of agricultural products, an increase over 1913 of 7,610,000; and in the same year they carried, of products of the mine,, forest, and factory, including merchandise, 78,391.000 tons, being a decrease from 1913 of 7,024,000 tons. It is evident therefore that the improvement in conditions referred to in the Speech from the Throne has been due entirely to the basic industry of agriculture. I have not the figures for 1925, but there is no doubt that for the tw'elve months just ended the result would be much more startling.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that there are a few lessons to be drawn from this state of affairs. Surely the most biased of protectionists in the Dominion, indeed those most ignorant of economics, must understand that statistics of this kind are not without significance. Canada has come to the point that England reached in 1845, when her manufacturers found their trade ruined by heavy taxes on food. This is very plainly stated in Trevelyan's Life of John Bright, and is part of a speech made in the British House of Commons on March 13, 1845. Now the old National Policy, which we have been labouring under since 1878, has at last put the cost of manufacturing so completely out of line with world prices that it is no longer possible to export manufactured goods except at a loss. While perhaps this was the case for several years before the war, the loss to the manufacturer then was probably not so great
that it could not be easily made up by charging the home consumer a price to cover all deficits-something we made possible by the import penalties we impose on our consuming public. To say that our manufacturers do not do this is to assert something which is entirely out of keeping with the facts. Take the case of automobiles. Our export trade has reached very respectable dimensions, and our manufacturers have not once told us that they cannot compete with their United States rivals in the Australian or New Zealand markets. I ask, then, why is it not possible for them to compete in the Canadian market without a tariff that gives them a price-fixing power over home buyers? Will the automobile manufacturer to-day say that he cannot compete with the foreign manufacturer here? If that is so, then he needs that price-fixing power just as much to meet competition in his overseas trade. Either he does not need that power in Canada, or else he is charging the home consumer a price to cover the deficit he suffers, say, in the Australian or New Zealand markets. I ask, which?
Do our manufacturers suffer a loss on their export trade, or are they carrying on their everlasting hypocritical whine in this House, session after session, for the purpose of fleecing the Canadian public? Again I ask, which? And perhaps some hon. member who follows me in this debate may be able to fully answer my question. I hope so. I assert, Sir, that there is no loss on their export trade. Therefore the tariff policy which the people have had to put up with since 1878 is a diabolical frame-up-a frame-up between the manufacturers and politicians for the purpose of fleecing the home consumer. The primary producer, the agriculturist chiefly, has had to bear the whole load. Will any one in this House tell me why the Canadian millers, for instance, need fifty cents a barrel protection on their flour, when Canadian flour can be, and very often is, sold cheaper in Great Britain than at the mills located on the wheat fields of Saskatchewan and Alberta, where we raise the finest wheat in the world? Millers have told me that it is because they put a much finer product on the Canadian market than they send abroad. Such is not the case. In fact, the best of everything goes to the British market, and because of her free trade policy Great Britain exploits the whole world for her food products, and only the best is sent there. Let me ask another question: Have the implement companies and other manufacturers - been exporting their wares to all parts of the world against the competition
The Address-Mr. Evans

of foreign manufacturers, and yet are not able to compete in the Canadian market with those manufacturers? No! a thousand' times no! A direct misrepresentation again. They have carried on a campaign of falsehood for greed, because forty-eight years ago corrupt politicians found it a convenient source of campaign funds-and to this day it is used for the same purpose. Lest I may appear too presumptuous in this statement, I should like to quote one or two authorities. My first quotation is from a speech by Sir Richard Cartwright, delivered in this House April 11, 1S90:
Finding we were not going to tax the people, the leader of the present government made an appeal to a set of gentlemen who put themselves up for sale, and who, the moment I refused to buy them, went and sold themselves to hon. gentlemen opposite. Yes, that is what they did. There never was an elector who sold himself for five dollars, who sold himself more completely than the protected manufacturers of Canada sold themselves to hon. gentlemen opposite. We did not buy them; and they sold themselves and their votes to hon. gentlemen opposite.
Goldwin Smith, another great Canadian, in his well-known work, Canada and the Canadian Question, said:
International hatred and political corruption are two inseparable companions of the system of protection. . . The upshot is that on the neck of the Canadian, as of the American commonwealth, now rides an association of protected manufacturers, making the community and all the great interests of the country tributary to their gain. Before a general election the Prime Minister calls these men together in the parlour of a Toronto hotel, receives their contributions to his election fund, and pledges the commercial policy of the country.
Up to 1S96 the Conservative party in power was responsible for the fiscal policy of this Dominion, and the history of the tariff for that period shows that an entirely one-sided arrangement was made for the benefit of manufacturers who could exercise political influence, Edward Porritt, the writer of Sixty Years of Protection in Canada is emphatic in declaring that it was again and again affirmed that the manufacturers subsidized the Conservative party to corral consumers by the tariff and compel them to buy their wares and pay the prices which the import penalties enabled them to exact. From the House of Commons debates of April 11, 1890,1 take this incident. Sir Richard Cartwright said that in the National Policy there was a duty of one cent a pound on rice, in the interest of two mills at which imported paddy rice was cleaned. He said that by this duty, $170,000 was fraudulently extracted from the pockets of the people, and that of this sum $10,000 to $15,000 was annually turned over at Red Parlour conferences by those who devised the

robbery, for the development of the election fund. When he said this Mackenzie Bowell said:
You don't mean that.
Sir Richard Cartwright answered:
I mean every word of it. I know how you do it
He continued:
I say that the whole business of protection is robbery, legalized robbery; that you subsidize the manufacturers and that the manufacturers in return subsidize you.
He also said that it was openly done by both parties to the transaction. Goldwin Smith in 1891 wrote:
"There is continual running to Ottawa for larger draughts of the fatal stimulant, when the first draught has failed."
It is a fact and it is a feature of protection that the thing can never be definite; it creates its own appetite and must be increased to be effective.
I will deal with that later on. Such, Mr. Speaker, is a short history of the background of our fiscal policy, and a bit of the history of the system on which the right hon. leader of the opposition and his party deem it an honour to have been elected. Let me quote his words, from page 211 of Hansard. He said:
Hon. gentlemen opposite know, and this whole House knows, that the party which I have the honour to lead to-night was sustained on the great issue of protection.

maintopic: GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Hon. gentlemen are proud
of that, but I am not at all envious. The right hon. gentleman when challenging the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) later on, when that gentleman declared that those from Quebec on the government side had been elected on a low tariff, asked how that policy was described. I want to say a word here about the way politics in this country are laid before the people, particularly this policy which makes legal the plunder of the people. I want to say here that the whole plan of campaign and organization of the Progressive party to-day is a challenge to all political leaders. Our electors themselves organized, formulated their own policies and elected their own representatives to advocate those policies in this House. That is the way in which it should be done, and the only way democracy can be maintained. I say it is a challenge to the political leaders and reformers of Canada to-day, to conduct their own political campaigns likewise. I will make the assertion here that if the question of protection had been honestly placed before this country during the last forty years, hardly one protectionist advo-
4S9

The Address-Mr. Evans
cate would have been returned an the last election. The organization of the people for their own information is the last thing the party politician would think of in the years gone by. I say to those advocates of privilege to-day that they are 5 p.m. afraid to organize their electors and let them meet to formulate their own principles and send their own representatives to this House. I challenge them to do it. I say again that the policy and plan of organization of the Progressive party constitute a challenge to this whole House.
That some advocates of protection are time and again elected is due to several causes, some of which I will name. One cause is the control of newspapers and magazines, the dissemination of literature by industrialists seeking class privilege, such as the woollen manufacturers, the writer of the Seeley national policy, the Prosperity League of Canada, and others. A strict silence, too, has been maintained for many years by professors of economy in all our colleges and universities; these institutions have come under the icy hand of privilege as completely as every other activity of this nation. There is also another means by which protectionists are elected to this House, and I do not know but that it may constitute the chief means-that is, the intimidation of workers in the industrial centres. Coupled with that is the continued threat of the capitalists to withdraw their investments if things do not go according to their wishes- and I want to say a word here regarding capital in relation to protection. I want to speak on that subject because I see concentrated to my right the representatives of organized industry and capital. Industry in this country has enjoyed the benefit of import penalties coupled with an arrangement under which raw material mostly comes in free since the Rays of Sir A. T. Galt, that is from about 1859. But I want to say that throughout this long period the system has had an entirely opposite effect from that for which it was inaugurated. In the first, place it has not, as vTas intended, kept the money in the country. We have borrowed more money for industrial purposes as a nation than perhaps any other nation on earth. Great Britain offers a striking contrast to that; she lends freely for industrial purposes to every other country in the world. I will make this further statement, Mr. Speaker, that the advocates for protection in Canada do not believe in their own policy. The one great thing we need, they all say, is capital to develop our own natural resources. Yet, we
see our directors of banking and finance investing in foreign enterprises in preference to developing our own natural resources; and one of the most glaring cases in point, one which was a real humiliation to us in the days of the war was the fact that while we produced as much as eighty-five per cent of the world's nickel we did not have a nickel refinery in Canada worthy of the name. Because of this lack our enemy was using nickel produced from Canadian ore and sold to it by foreign refiners.

maintopic: GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman give us some proof of that?

maintopic: GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: It is well known.

maintopic: GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Give us proof.

maintopic: GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I have not the proof here
but it is a fact all the same. The proof is that it was mentioned in this House in 1922-

maintopic: GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: And contradicted.

maintopic: GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
-and some help was given by the Canadian government towards the production of nickel. That was in the session of 1922 and I was a member at the time. Let me give another instance which goes to show the perfidy of our protectionist advocates to their own doctrine. To-day we are supplying a very large part of the world's pulpwood. To-day our manufacturers are calling for an export embargo on this raw material. Instead of controlling the world's markets by their own foresight and enterprise they ask to be placed entirely beyond the competition of the foreigner by an export embargo. This would give them a pricefixing power over the pulpwood producer who would be unmercifully exploited, just as the miller is seeking an embargo on wheat to-day in order to have the farmer delivered a little more completely over to his mercy that he may the more easily skim the cream off the crop. Protection is in many ways hindering the development of this nation. There are two particularly disastrous features which always accompany a system of privilege as a national policy. First, it destroys enterprise, it is detrimental in this respect even to those whom it was supposed to benefit. That is plainly shown to-day, I think, in the demand for export embargoes. It also destroys courage and self-reliance. As a result our manufacturers to-day are relying on the tariff to secure a market for them rather than having recourse to their own enterprise and the quality of their goods. I think this is plainly seen in the fact that 116 men elected to this House are plaintively calling
The Address-Mr. Evans

on parliament to stand between them and the competition of the foreigner.

maintopic: GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: A competition of low wages.

maintopic: GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: They are proud of it, evidently.

maintopic: GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Evidently. Not only has
this system been detrimental to their own self-reliance and enterprise, but they have used this national charity to destroy the enterprise of the small proprietor. They have absorbed the little industries of the small proprietors, and concentrated them under their own exploiting control. I think it is no exaggeration to say that every small industry in the province of Ontario has been cornered by fair or foul means. Furthermore, the small industries of the Maritime provinces too have been closed out by unfair methods of competition, until those provinces to-day have become hewers of wood and drawers of water for this industrial area situated between Montreal and Windsor.

maintopic: GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Oh, oh!

maintopic: GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Some hon. gentlemen know that to be quite true, but in view of where they are sitting, they do not like to admit it. The other disastrous feature of this national indulgence is that it has impoverished the primary industries of the country, and particularly the basic industry of agriculture. Protection to be effective must always be parasitic in its nature. It cannot be anything else; it can only live by obtaining that for which it gives nothing in return; it lives practically on the blood of others. Protection for manufacturers is effective because agriculture cannot be protected; and hon. gentlemen may as well get it out of their heads that they are going to persuade the agriculturist of this country that agriculture can be protected by a high tariff. It is a common economic law that the industry that creates the new wealth of any country must find its market in the wide world and accept world's prices for its products. Agriculture is impoverished because the manufacturer is not standing on his own feet but is dependent on the tax laid on the consumer to give him a profit on what he sells at home and abroad.
This fact and the way it affects agriculture has made necessary the scheme of rural credits. Indeed, any one perusing the Speech from the Throne must surely be struck by the fact that all our problems are inseparable-that is there is an underlying cause for

them all. This system is also the cause of the great need for immigration; it necessitates our young men leaving Canada and seeking their fortunes in other countries. The agriculturist of Canada to-day could find employment for every idle man in the country could he pay the wages commensurate with the high cost of living. This is not possible because the cost of production in Canada is out of line with world prices. We are crippling the development of this nation by that fallacious policy which we have followed for the last sixty years. It is not possible for the farmer to pay that wage because the cost of production in Canada is entirely out of line with world prices. The production and distribution of this country has actually become too expensive to permit our people to look after even their own natural products. The right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) sought to persuade the agriculturists that he could give them a price-fixing power. We are to-day seeking a market abroad for nearly 400 million bushels of wheat and we have got to do that in the world's market. What a fallacy then to think that he can protect the farmer. How is he going to do it? I repeat, what a fallacy! In>
fact the whole idea of protection is a fallacy, but perhaps the people of the cities will never realize this until the time comes when .the agriculturist can demand his own price.
Much has been said in this debate about the importation of butter and eggs. I do not think the farmers are complaining much. In this respect the Australian treaty has been cited as a gross injustice. On the face of it,
I admit it is an injustice to certain classes, But I want the people to understand that trade treaties are always an injustice to the primary producers of any country that finds it necessary to make trade treaties. The trade treaties are essentially a feature of countries imposing protection on their consumers. A free trade country makes no treaties. It cannot. It has nothing to bargain with.

maintopic: GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: It does not have to.

maintopic: GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
As the hon. member says, it does not have to. They are not needed. Trade treaties are a part of the class privilege as much as the import penalties themselves are. A trade treaty can be of advantage to privileged classes in Canada only by trading the rights of the agriculturists to give them an advantage in foreign markets. In the Australian treaty the rights of the farmers have to some extent been sacrificed by placing their

The Address-Mr. Evans
products on the free list in order to give the Canadian manufacturer of automobiles, agricultural implements, pulp products and other things a preference in the Australian market. The leader of the opposition last session and during the election campaign, urged the adoption of a higher protection on butter, eggs, poultry, vegetables and so on. This again was even a more seductive way of increasing the draught of the fatal stimulant of protection, the inevitable reaction of which must fall on the agriculturist. If the agriculturist would agree to that part of the deceptive game, those who desire more advantage under price fixing tariffs would have an excuse to demand higher import penalties for their own goods. It seems that it worked very well in the United States some time ago as an excuse for the Fordney tariff. But even if this protection for the farmer proved beneficial, it could only be so for a short time, very short at that, as wages would have to be increased to meet the higher cost. Manufacturing would be more costly, distribution costs would have to be increased, and the farmer again would find himself going round in the same old circle. In such a demand the hollowness of the protectionist's argument is very plainly revealed. If these things are cheap now to the consumer, that must of itself prove of advantage to the manufacturer. If anything would prove conducive to making this country a manufacturing country, surely it is the low cost of living. Why then do they want to increase it? I say it is simply because they want an excuse to increase their own protection.
Protection can only be effective when an effective system of immigration is carried on alongside, and a gradual but continuous lowering of living standards for the workers to a point where the low wage balances the greed of the employer. The fact that the present rate does not give the desired protection or the price-fixing power is due to the completeness of the workers' organization, and hence the feverish anxiety for immigration. It is not borne out by facts that a country to be prosperous must have a large population. England to-day wants to get rid of a number of her men. The question at present is not how to get immigrants. The real question we should consider to-day is what becomes of our earnings. Here is the crux of the whole situation. This year we shall in all probability exceed all countries in the amount of exports per head of population, yet those who raise this new wealth will be left as poor as they were before, and nothing looking to a permanence of manufacture or agriculture will be
instituted. In all probability we shall this year raise some $125,000,000 by the tariff. To do that we shall have fleeced our people of about $375,000,000, $250,000,000 of which will go into the pockets of the protected interests, or as the ratio of home manufactured goods stands to imported commodities consumed in Canada. I will quote the computation given by Sir Richard Cartwright at the 1893 Liberal convention held in this city. Any hon. member can find it at page 42. He said:
The cost of protection to the people of Canada between 1880 and 1893 is hardly less than $1,000,000,000.
During those thirteen years the protective tariff took out of the pockets of the people as much as $76,000,000 annually, and this was when our population wa3 considerably under five millions and prices only a little over one-half of what they are to-day. The national debt and the railway debt of this country pale into insignificance in comparison with the amount we put into the pockets of the protected interests. The national debt to-day could be wiped out in ten years with what we are taking from the pockets of our workers. The amount pocketed by those for whom this robbery was devised is not by any means the whole of the evil. It is crippling the basic industry of the country, the one industry that can stand on its feet. There is only one brake on production on our farms, and that is the high cost of production. The hon. member for East Toronto (Mr. Ryckman) crystallized this very well in a statement which he made in the last session of the last parliament, that Toronto itself was paying twenty-three per cent of the income tax of the whole Dominion. That is a most startling statement, but I do not dispute his words. I think what he meant to throw at this part of the House was the fact that somehow we were beating the income tax collector. Such is not the case. We would very much like to have an opportunity of paying income tax; but the evil today is this concentration of wealth and industry in the hands of a few who are directing every activity of the nation. That statement of the hon. gentleman was, however, an admission in regard to those in the city of Toronto who were paying twenty-three per cent of the income tax of the Dominion. We have heard it stated several times in this House that those industries on which that great income was made could not live without this price-fixing power which this country gives them. That means that this country is taxing itself to keep those industries in Toronto, and as we used to say in the Old Country, anyone living on the taxes is a pauper. Thus we are face to face with, perhaps, one of the
The Address-Mr. Evans

worst incongruities ever known in a national way, when we permit our paupers to pay our income tax.
But to pass on, let me say that rural credits as a national benefit will be rendered null and void under this system of concentration of wealth. The Empire Settlement scheme itself cannot function under such a policy of concentration of the nation's earnings. It has often been said that our tariff is very low, and I admit that the tariff schedule is an innocent looking document. In fact the whole Customs tariff is not by any means a formidable thing, although it is all one-eidedi and discriminatory. But the departmental rules and orders in council governing the administration of the act, which are seldom exposed to the public gaze, constitute something altogether different. Let me give the House one or two instances, and first let me take the case of trade discounts. The figures which I am going to give have been submitted to a tariff expert and he has found them to be correct. If we take the case of household utensils as an example, I find that the rules of the manufacturers and distributing combines are recognized in the administration of the act. As an example, the price to all is say $100. To the large dealer there is a discount of 50 per cent and 15 per cqnt and 10 per cent, leaving a value for duty of $38.25. The duty on that is $11.47 and the sales tax $2.98, making a total cost to the large dealer, mark the figures of $52.70. To the jobber there is a discount of 50 and 15 and 20 per cent, making the cost for duty $34.01. The duty in that case is $10.20, and the sales tax $2.65, making the total cost of $46.86. To the departmental store the total cost would be $49.71. To the consumer, however, the valuation for customs purposes is $100. It does not matter what he has bought them for or what discount has been allowed, the department does not allow any trade discount to enter into the appraisement for the purpose of imposing a duty. It does not matter what the quantity the consumer buys may be, the valuation for duty is $100. The duty would be $30 and the sales tax $7.80, making a total cost of $137.80. The tariff schedule innocently names 30 per cent as the duty to be paid as protection. In practice, it works out at from 90 to 190 per cent according to the classifications.
The Customs tariff is administered in a way that is not known to the public, secretly and tyrannically in the interests of those who are in partnership with the politicians. The manufacturers and distributing combines have made a set of rules which they compel the politicians to accept and establish by orders in

council, all designed to make the consumer pay the bill. But I have something worse yet, and this touches, perhaps, the very quick, the very heart of any man who has any sense of the liberty that he should enjoy. Under the rules of the combines in Canada to-day, no co-operative company can get a better standing than a consumer and it must pay the consumer's price. It does not matter what line of business a co-operative company may carry on or the extent of its buying and selling, it is still a consumer. It does not matter at what price it may buy its goods in a foreign country, the value set by the customs appraiser in this country is the value which the Canadian combine controlling that particular line says that it ought to be. What do you think of that in a democratic country? If the consumers of Canada think that they are free they are mistaken, for the Canadian public does not know what liberty is. Since 1878 we have handed ourselves over to a set of men who are controlling every activity in the country; they control price and everything else, and they control the lives of the workers of this land. This very system has closed some of the best co-operative companies in western Canada. The price set by the customs appraiser is always the retailer's price to the consumer. I should like the people to take to heart this fact, that cooperative companies, no matter how much business they do or whatever line of goods they distribute, are always classed as consumers, and under the combines rules it is forbidden to sell any class of goods or merchandise to a co-operative company. This is what has crippled the co-operative companies in Canada. They are compelled to go abroad for their goods, buying their supplies in foreign countries, and they are subject to the Dumping Act. The co-operative company being classed as a consumer has to pay, under the Dumping Act, a duty equal to all the profits of the other classes above him, that is to say, the retailer, the wholesaler, the dealer, the jobber or the manufacturer, as well as the difference in price between what the foreign manufacturer charges and what the Canadian manufacturer says it ought to be.
I submit to the House that this is the most diabolical piece of legislation ever enacted in modem times. Canada was the first of all countries in all time to conceive such an idea and this act was placed on the statute books for the first time in the year 1904. It was vigorously enforced between 1911 and 1918 but it was not until 1922 that it completely covered every line of merchandise that the consumer needs, even to his daily bread. That

The Address-Mr. Evans
amendment passed this House by the combined strength of the Liberal and Conservative parties against the solid vote of the Progressives.

maintopic: GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: What year was that?

maintopic: GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: It was on June 23, 1922.

maintopic: GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I would never support
a government like that.

maintopic: GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The right hon. gentleman
himself denounced it as protection of protection. He denounced the government in language such as I had never heard used to a public body, and yet he and his party afterwards unanimously voted for the whole thing.

maintopic: GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
We denounced them for
their treachery but not for the principle. The hon. gentleman however supported them for both.

maintopic: GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: My right hon. friend very aptly described the legislation and I would commend the House to a reading of his words at that time. He was even more denunciatory than I have been myself to-day. I have spent some time discussing this question, but when I hear so many members on the Conservative side glibly talking protection, and the right hon. gentleman declaring his pride in being leader of a party elected because of its stand on this question, then I wonder if even these hon. gentlemen know the extent of the bondage under which they have placed the country. Stability has almost become a slogan in this House during the last three or four years. Let me say to those who believe in creating stable conditions by oppression that it cannot be done. Whether you have a tariff commission or a tariff advisory board, or whether you take the tariff out of politics or do what you like, stability cannot be created by oppression. It is as true to-day as when Lincoln uttered these words in reference to his own country, that this nation cannot live with one-half free and the other half slaves. If there is an industry to-day that cannot live by its own perseverance and enterprise, let it lay its books on the table and if it is essential to the welfare of the country that it should be helped in some way then let it be helped. Since an advisory tariff board is to be appointed I hope it may do some good in this direction, but I have very little hope of it.

maintopic: GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Do you believe in a (policy of absolute free trade for Canada?

maintopic: GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I believe that the policy of protection has nearly driven us to the wall.
Under the tariff we have created a set of exotic industries that cannot stand a breath of fresh air. The whole discussion here on Monday centred round an industry that had been established on a basis of tariffs, bonuses and bounties-the British Empire Steel Corporation and particularly the steal concerns.
I am in favour of free trade for Canada. We have established our industries on a false foundation, and on the statement of the leader of the opposition, I say they are beginning to tumble down around our heads and we are on all fours trying to keep on top of the debris to-day.

maintopic: GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I hope the hon. member will not be found voting for a Speech from the Throne which declares that we are in a very flourishing condition.

maintopic: GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I am quoting what the right hon. gentleman himself said. Two sessions ago in this House he said that 2,000 factories had been closed in one year. Well, I happen to know something of the reason why some of these factories were closed. I have said the same thing in the House before, and at the risk of tedious repetition I shall say it again: the name of the Libby-Owens Company was frequently mentioned two years ago as one that had failed because insufficient protection had been given to it. Now let me tell the House something. In one of the large buildings in course of erection in western Canada, a sanatorium, there are three large sunrooms running the whole length of the structure, some 200 feet. I was up there one day and noticing that the boxes were all labelled England or Belgium, I asked the foreman: "Why is it that you did not get this stuff in Canada and so give employment to Canadians? A company in Hamilton has closed down because it had not sufficient trade." " Oh yes," he replied, " I know, they are the Libby-Owens Company; but we could not use their stuff, it was too brittle." There was another case. As I said before, our manufacturers are lying down under the tariff, expecting that to carry them through rather than the quality of their goods and their own enterprise. The whole thing is a fallacy. I am rather surprised at the leader of the opposition supporting this system as he does, year after year.

maintopic: GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: He knows better.

maintopic: GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Of course he does. But this is what I want to say:	Surely the day is
gone by when this nation will give any in-
The Address-Mr. Evans

dustry increased power under the system of the past to exploit the public and harass too, the primary producer with high prices, which he is compelled to meet by long hours of toil and a low standard of living. We have the finest country on the face of God's earth,-	t

maintopic: GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
-and a freedom to develop the agricultural industry, the one basic industry of this country, would populate our empty spaces, and secondary industries to supply the agriculturists with what they need would then grow up naturally. I think there is the best answer to the hon. gentleman who asked me if I believed in free trade. Our industrial system has been built up by hothouse methods, and cannot stand the natural air of competition. We must get rid of the thing in our midst, class legislation-class privilege-which is dividing the different classes, the different vocations and the various geographical areas of this Dominion, even to the extent of breaking up confederation.
It has been said that Canada with its diversified areas and climate is a hard country to govern, I want to say to this House that it is only a hard country to govern according to the extent that class privilege is permitted to divide classes and areas, I want to say to each man and to each class conducting the different activities of this country:	Let each
mind his own business, and not prey on his neighbour by feudalistic means established by legislation. Then we shall have peace. We may have our political differences, but let us get rid1 of this thing that divides us, and so develop a common nationality, a common love of country, and implant in the people a tradition of kinship. Government should be based on a square deal to all. But our parliament is a disgrace; it has been reduced to nothing better than a plunderbund, and government has become a mercenary scramble.

maintopic: GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to add my congratulations to those which have already been tendered to you and to the mover and seconder of the Address. I am glad that J still have this privilege left to me, for it is about the only time-honoured practice which has survived the general slaughter of constitutional precedents and traditions and customs in this House. The honour conferred on you, Sir, is all the greater because it is a departure^ for the first time since confederation, from the' well-established _ rule that representatives of the two principal races should alternately
JMr. Evans.]
occupy that honourable position. I hasten to remark that with the creation of this new precedent I am not disposed to find fault. At all events I can assure you of this, Sir,- and I am certain that I also speak the sentiment of every hon. member in this section of the House-that I would far rather see you occupying the position which you are so eminently qualified to fill than any hon. gentleman who sits to your right. But, Mr. Speaker, I had doubts whether you would be re-elected to that position. I recall that years ago, at the conclusion of the war, Sir Robert Borden manifested to a remarkable degree that rarest of all virtues, political gratitude, by appointing to honourable positions several who had been faithful to him in the time of crisis. Some were appointed to the Senate; some to the bench; two in particular were singled out for special honour, because, as you will recall, Sir, they had for many, many years manifested an almost violent affection for the Conservative party-one was made chairman of the Board of Railway Commissioners, the other was appointed a lieutenant-governor. I thought that the Liberal party would not wish to be outdone in practising this rare virtue of political gratitude. There are gentlemen in this House whose services, in season and out of season, deserve appreciation, and I really thought that the chair which you now fill might perhaps be occupied by the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke), or possibly by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland), or the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speakman); I even thought that if ex-Premier King's chivalry was equal to that high sense of honour with which he was credited1 by the Minister of Customs (Mr. Boivin) the other day, the member for Southeast Grey (Miss Mac-Phail) might stand a very good chance of becoming Speaker of this" chamber. However, chivalry is a thing of the past apparently, and political gratitude came to an end with Sir Robert Borden's practise of that virtue.
Now,^ Mr. Speaker, there are one or twc things in the address to which we have just listened that I should like >to draw attention to before you call it six o'clock. The hon. member for Rosetown (Mr. Evans) is in a position of splendid isolation in this House so far as tariff matters are concerned.

maintopic: GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Not isolated, no.

maintopic: GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Very much so, I 'think. His mind is dominated by theoretical assumptions and arguments which, oft repeated, have become ingrained and occupy a segregated area of grey matter to the exclusion of everything

The Address-Mr. Evans
except the theories of Adam Smith and Cobden. I have not the pleasure or privilege of knowing the hon. gentleman, but I had always understood that he was noted for his sincerity and earnestness. I believe that most people in this country gave him credit for those qualities, but I am rather disposed to think that his sincerity will have to be discounted in view of his attitude recently. I have in my hand the report of a speech made by him on September 25 last, in which he says:
There can be no coalition as long as the Liberal party is wallowing in the mire of corruption, as it is.
"No coalition," the hon. gentleman says, but he has already shown his willingness to co-operate with the Liberal party in corruption. No coalition with the Liberal party in corruption; but co-operation with them in corruption.

maintopic: GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: May I ask the hon. gentleman if a coalition has been entered into?

maintopic: GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I am taking the hon. gentleman's statement that he was not prepared to enter into a coalition with the Liberal party while it was' wallowing in corruption, and I am adding to that this further statement-which is a statement of fact-that he has already manifested in this House his readiness to co-operate with the Liberal party which he says is wallowing in corruption. How far the hon. gentleman has to travel 'between co-operation and coalition is something that he will have to work out for himself.

maintopic: GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Another question, please.
The hon. gentleman has not yet shown my hypocrisy or insincerity in the matter, and perhaps he might tell me-

maintopic: GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: What is the question?

maintopic: GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I would like to ask my hon. friend to name the course I should have taken to be sincere?

maintopic: GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I do not think there should be any doubt in the hon. gentleman's mind in that connection. We have his declaration that this government is wallowing in corruption. Surely a man with any moral sense would know that the right course would be to vote against a party which was wallowing in corruption. The hon. gentleman should not need any guidance in that. And allow me to quote a little further. He said in the same speech:
One of the vi'.est untruths that any politician was ever guilty of, Mr. Evans asserted, had been uttered by Hon. W. R. Motherwell when he told a Saskatoon audience in 1923 that the government has reduced duties on sixty commodities.
Yet he lines up with the Minister of Agriculture in the only vote which has so far been taken in this House. Again he says:
I challenge the Liberal party to go out and carry on a campaign of education along the lines of its own platform, and to choose its candidates in a democratic way.
He had no faith in the Liberal party, evidently, nor in the Liberal platform; he challenges them to the issue, but when he comes into this House he goes back on his professions and lines up with a party, one of whose ministers he says tells vile untruths, and a party which he says is wallowing in corruption. It is apparently good enough for the hon. member for Rosetown to associate with. The hon. gentleman, speaking on the same occasion, further said:
The only difference between the Conservative and Liberal parties is that the Conservatives openly advocate class privilege through protection, while the Liberals achieved this end through stealth ever since 1896.
So if we may judge from the hon. gentleman's attitude, he does not prefer the open way, but rather desires to associate with those who gain their ends by stealth and underhand methods. He says further in the same speech:
The Liberals have gone even further in the extension of class privilege than the Conservatives. The Liberal government, by administering the Customs Act in secret, has gone further in increasing tariff charges than any government since 1867.
In the face of these words, Mr. Speaker, what would any person not acquainted with the hon. gentleman expect his course to have been? The last thing one would have expected would be that a gentleman of his fine type would associate himself with a government wallowing in corruption, one of whose members he charges with uttering vile untruths, a party which attained its ends by stealth instead of by open, manly and aboveboard methods. Yet we find the hon. gentleman apparently ready to swallow not only his own convictions and principles, but to swallow the whole government, or what is left of it, on the other side of the House. I will refer further to the hon. gentleman's speech on another occasion.
On motion of Mr. Edwards (Frontenac-Addington) the debate was adjourned.
At six o'clock the House adjourned, without question being put, pursuant to rule.

Adjournment of the House
